The Caspian tyulka Clupeonella caspia is a small, short-lived clupeid endemic to the Caspian Sea, where it plays a central role in the pelagic food web. Field surveys indicate that this species attains an ultimate total length of 14.9 cm [Li = 14.9 cm], a modest size typical of the genus. Growth trajectories derived from otolith readings suggest that most individuals achieve this asymptotic length within their first two years. The species exhibits relatively rapid somatic development, with puberty—defined as the onset of gonadal recrudescence and the capacity to produce gametes—occurring once individuals reach a total length of 8.8 cm [Lp = 8.8 cm]. This length-based threshold at maturation is consistent with patterns observed in other small planktivorous fish from the Ponto-Caspian region, where early maturation is favored under conditions of high natural mortality and seasonal productivity pulses.

Reproductive output in Caspian tyulka, as in many iteroparous clupeids, varies seasonally with thermal conditions. In laboratory aquaria maintained at a constant temperature of 28.5 °C [T = 28.5 °C], the gonadosomatic index (GSI) for actively spawning females reaches a peak value of 30% [GSI = 30%]. This elevated index indicates a substantial investment in gamete production under warm, stable thermal regimes. By contrast, field collections across the annual cycle show that the average GSI across the population peaks at a lower value of 10% [GSI = 10%]. The disparity between laboratory and field values underscores the thermal sensitivity of reproductive physiology in this species.

Embryonic and larval development in the Caspian tyulka proceeds rapidly under warm conditions. At a water temperature of 28.5 °C [T = 28.5 °C], the incubation period is brief, with hatched larvae emerging from the chorion just three days [ab = three days] after fertilisation. Such a short developmental window is advantageous in a highly variable pelagic environment where predation pressure on egg stages is intense. The resulting yolk-sac larva is minute, with an initial wet weight at birth of 0.00027 grams [Wwb = 0.00027 grams], a mass that reflects the small diameter of the pelagic eggs. This limited endogenous yolk supply necessitates a rapid transition to exogenous feeding; larvae must encounter suitable planktonic prey within a few hours of mouth opening to avoid starvation, consistent with the high mortality rates typical of the early larval phase in marine and estuarine clupeids.

Longevity data from mark-recapture programs and otolith-based aging indicate that the Caspian tyulka is a short-lived species, with a maximum lifespan at ambient temperatures averaging around 28.5 °C [T = 28.5 °C] of eight years [am = eight years]. This relatively short lifespan is typical of small, fast-growing clupeids that face intense predation from piscivorous fish such as the Caspian seal and several sturgeon species. The ultimate wet weight attained by adults is approximately 16.45 grams [Wwi = approximately 16.45 grams], a mass that is reached when individuals achieve their asymptotic length. At puberty, when fish reach a total length of 8.8 cm [Lp = 8.8 cm], the corresponding body mass is roughly 3.42 grams [Wwp = roughly 3.42 grams], representing a substantial fraction of the ultimate mass and highlighting the energetic investment required before reproductive capability is established.

Reproductive output in the Caspian tyulka is partitioned across multiple spawning events within a single year during the warm season. The species is capable of producing three separate spawnings per year [F_R_i = three separate spawnings per year], with each spawning event yielding a batch of pelagic eggs. The population-level average gonadosomatic index peaks at approximately 10% [GSI = 10%] during the height of the spawning season. This iteroparous strategy, with multiple spawning bouts, buffers the population against the stochastic survival of any single larval cohort and is a common adaptation among small pelagic fish inhabiting seasonally productive ecosystems. The combination of a modest ultimate length of 14.9 cm [Li = 14.9 cm], a moderate adult mass of approximately 16.45 grams [Wwi = approximately 16.45 grams], and a lifespan not exceeding eight years [am = eight years] positions the species firmly within the fast end of the life-history continuum at a temperature of 28.5 °C [T = 28.5 °C].
